first_memory.longDescription: Your first step into persistent memory with Claude Code. Creating a CLAUDE.md file establishes a knowledge base that Claude reads at the start of every conversation. This file can contain project context, coding preferences, workflow guidelines, and any information you want Claude to remember across sessions. Think of it as giving Claude a briefing document before each interaction.
first_memory.whyItMatters: Without CLAUDE.md, Claude starts every session with zero context about your project or preferences. This file is the foundation for all other memory features.

howTo.summary: Create a CLAUDE.md file in your project root or user config directory

steps.instruction: Create a project-level CLAUDE.md in your repository root

code.content: touch CLAUDE.md

steps.instruction: Add some basic content about your project

code.content:
# Project Guidelines

This is a Node.js REST API using Express and TypeScript.

## Key Information
- Use npm, not yarn
- Tests use Jest
- Database is PostgreSQL

steps.instruction: Start a new Claude Code session - Claude will automatically read this file

examples.title: Minimal Project Memory
examples.description: A simple starting point for any project

code.content:

## Stack

- Backend: Express.js
- Database: MongoDB

examples.explanation: Even minimal context helps Claude make better suggestions aligned with your tech stack.

tips: Start simple - you can always add more content later
Claude reads CLAUDE.md at conversation start, so changes take effect on the next session

personal_scribe.longDescription: Establish your personal coding identity by creating a user-level CLAUDE.md file. This file lives in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and applies to ALL your Claude Code sessions, regardless of which project you're working on. Perfect for documenting your universal preferences like preferred languages, coding style, communication preferences, and tools you always use.
personal_scribe.whyItMatters: User-level memory ensures Claude knows your personal preferences everywhere, eliminating the need to repeat yourself in every project.

howTo.summary: Create CLAUDE.md in your ~/.claude directory for global preferences

steps.instruction: Create the .claude directory if it doesn't exist

code.content: mkdir -p ~/.claude

steps.instruction: Create your personal CLAUDE.md file

code.content: touch ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md

steps.instruction: Add your personal preferences and style guide

code.content:
# My Coding Preferences

## Language & Style
- Prefer TypeScript over JavaScript
- Use functional programming patterns when possible
- Always add JSDoc comments to exported functions

## Communication
- Be concise in explanations
- Show code examples rather than lengthy descriptions

## Tools
- Use pnpm for package management
- Prefer Vitest over Jest for testing

examples.title: Personal Style Guide

code.content:
# Personal Preferences

## Code Style
- 2-space indentation
- Single quotes for strings
- Trailing commas in multi-line arrays/objects
- Prefer async/await over .then() chains

## When Writing Code
- Include error handling
- Add TypeScript types, avoid 'any'
- Write self-documenting code with clear variable names

examples.explanation: These preferences apply to every project you work on with Claude Code.

tips: Keep user-level preferences general - project-specific details belong in project CLAUDE.md
User preferences are merged with project preferences, with project taking priority for conflicts

project_memory.longDescription: Create a project-specific CLAUDE.md file that lives in your repository root. This file contains context unique to one project: architecture decisions, coding conventions, important file locations, deployment processes, and team agreements. Unlike user-level memory, project memory can be shared with your team through version control.
project_memory.whyItMatters: Project-level memory keeps Claude aligned with your specific codebase conventions and can be shared across your entire team for consistent AI assistance.

howTo.summary: Create CLAUDE.md in your project root with project-specific guidelines

steps.instruction: Create CLAUDE.md in your project root directory

code.content: touch ./CLAUDE.md

steps.instruction: Document your project architecture and conventions

code.content:
# Project: E-Commerce API

## Architecture
- Monorepo with packages/ directory
- Each package is independently deployable
- Shared types in packages/shared

## Conventions
- Controllers in src/controllers/
- Services in src/services/
- Use dependency injection via tsyringe

## Commands
- `npm run dev` - Start development server
- `npm run test` - Run tests
- `npm run build` - Build for production

steps.instruction: Commit the file to share with your team

code.content: git add CLAUDE.md && git commit -m 'Add Claude Code project memory'

dual_wielder.longDescription: Master the memory hierarchy by maintaining both user-level and project-level CLAUDE.md files simultaneously. This setup gives you the best of both worlds: your personal preferences apply everywhere while project-specific rules override them when needed. Claude merges these files intelligently, applying user preferences first, then layering project preferences on top.
dual_wielder.whyItMatters: The dual-file approach lets you maintain consistent personal style while respecting each project's unique requirements and team conventions.

howTo.summary: Create and maintain both ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ./CLAUDE.md files

steps.instruction: Ensure you have a user-level CLAUDE.md with personal preferences

## My Style
- TypeScript with strict mode
- Functional patterns preferred
- Comprehensive error handling

## Communication
- Concise explanations
- Show code first, explain after

preference_keeper.longDescription: Document your personal coding style and preferences in CLAUDE.md. Preference Keeper celebrates the art of teaching Claude your unique coding DNA - whether you prefer tabs over spaces, functional over OOP, verbose over terse. These preferences help Claude generate code that feels like you wrote it yourself.
preference_keeper.whyItMatters: Documented preferences mean less time correcting Claude's output and more time building. Claude matches your style automatically.

howTo.summary: Document your coding preferences and style conventions in CLAUDE.md

steps.instruction: Consider your preferences across different dimensions
steps.note: Formatting, naming, patterns, libraries, verbosity, comments

steps.instruction: Create a preferences section with clear guidelines

code.content:
## Coding Preferences

### Formatting
- Use 2-space indentation
- Prefer single quotes for strings
- Always use trailing commas
- Max line length: 100 characters

### Naming Conventions
- Use camelCase for variables and functions
- Use PascalCase for classes and components
- Use SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for constants
- Prefix boolean variables with is/has/should

### Patterns
- Prefer async/await over Promise chains
- Use early returns to reduce nesting
- Prefer const over let when possible
- Use destructuring for object parameters

examples.title: Complete Style Preferences

code.content:
## My Coding Style

### I Prefer
- Functional programming over OOP
- Composition over inheritance
- Explicit over implicit
- Small functions (< 20 lines)
- Immutable data structures

### Always Use
- TypeScript strict mode
- ESLint with strict config
- Prettier for formatting

### Avoid
- Any type in TypeScript
- Nested callbacks
- Magic numbers (use named constants)
- Abbreviations in variable names

examples.explanation: Clear preferences guide Claude to generate code matching your exact style.

tips: Include both positive preferences (do this) and negative ones (avoid that)
Be specific about edge cases where your preference differs from common convention

forbidden_patterns.longDescription: Protect your codebase by documenting anti-patterns, deprecated approaches, and things to explicitly avoid. Forbidden Patterns helps you create guardrails that prevent Claude from using problematic code patterns, outdated libraries, or approaches that have caused issues in the past. These negative rules are just as valuable as positive guidance.
forbidden_patterns.whyItMatters: Explicit anti-patterns prevent Claude from repeating mistakes and keep deprecated or problematic code out of your codebase.

howTo.summary: Document anti-patterns and things to avoid using NEVER, DON'T, AVOID keywords

steps.instruction: Identify problematic patterns from past experience
steps.note: Deprecated APIs, security issues, performance problems, team decisions

steps.instruction: Create a dedicated section for things to avoid

code.content:
## Anti-Patterns - DO NOT USE

### NEVER
- NEVER use `any` type in TypeScript - always define proper types
- NEVER store secrets in code - use environment variables
- NEVER use `eval()` or `new Function()` - security risk
- NEVER mutate function parameters directly

### AVOID
- AVOID using `var` - use `const` or `let` instead
- AVOID nested ternaries - use if/else for complex logic
- AVOID default exports - use named exports for better refactoring

### DEPRECATED
- DO NOT use moment.js - use date-fns instead
- DO NOT use class components - use functional components with hooks
- DO NOT use enzyme - use React Testing Library

steps.instruction: Explain why something is forbidden when it's not obvious

code.content:
### Forbidden: jQuery
DO NOT use jQuery in this project.
Reason: We use React for DOM manipulation. jQuery conflicts with React's virtual DOM and causes unpredictable behavior.

examples.title: Security and Quality Guardrails

code.content:
## Prohibited Patterns

### Security
- NEVER use `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` without sanitization
- NEVER log sensitive data (passwords, tokens, PII)
- NEVER disable CORS in production

### Quality
- DON'T use console.log for debugging - use proper logger
- DON'T catch errors without handling them
- DON'T use magic strings - define constants

### Architecture
- AVOID direct database queries in controllers
- AVOID circular dependencies between modules
- DON'T import from parent directories (no ../..)

examples.explanation: Clear prohibitions with context help Claude avoid common pitfalls.

tips: Use strong language (NEVER, DON'T, AVOID) to signal importance
Include the reason why something is forbidden when it's a team/project decision

environment_detector.longDescription: Account for cross-platform differences by including platform-specific instructions in your CLAUDE.md. Environment Detector recognizes developers who work across macOS, Linux, and Windows, or who manage projects that need to behave differently in various environments. Document platform quirks, OS-specific commands, and environment-conditional behavior.
environment_detector.whyItMatters: Platform-aware instructions ensure Claude gives you the right commands and patterns regardless of which operating system you're using.

howTo.summary: Include platform-specific instructions using OS names or conditional patterns

steps.instruction: Identify platform-specific behaviors in your project
steps.note: File paths, shell commands, environment variables, package managers

steps.instruction: Document platform differences explicitly

code.content:
## Platform-Specific Notes

### macOS
- Use `brew` for system dependencies
- File paths are case-insensitive by default
- Use `open` command to open files/URLs

### Linux
- Use `apt` or `dnf` for system dependencies
- File paths are case-sensitive
- Use `xdg-open` for opening files/URLs

### Windows
- Use PowerShell or WSL for scripts
- Use `\` for path separators in native commands
- Environment variables: `%VAR%` (cmd) or `$env:VAR` (PowerShell)

steps.instruction: Add conditional instructions when needed

code.content:
## Development Setup

On macOS/Linux:
```bash
export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb"
npm run dev
```

On Windows (PowerShell):
```powershell
$env:DATABASE_URL="postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb"
npm run dev
```

examples.title: Cross-Platform Development Guide

code.content:
## Cross-Platform Notes

### File Paths
- Use `path.join()` in Node.js, never hardcode separators
- Store paths with forward slashes in config files

### Docker
- On macOS/Windows: Docker Desktop required
- On Linux: Native Docker installation

### Platform Detection
Use `process.platform` to check:
- `darwin` = macOS
- `linux` = Linux
- `win32` = Windows

examples.explanation: Platform awareness prevents OS-specific bugs and incorrect command suggestions.

tips: Focus on differences that actually affect development workflow
Test commands on all platforms your team uses

conditional_memory.longDescription: Create dynamic, context-aware instructions using conditional language in your CLAUDE.md. Conditional Memory allows you to specify different behaviors based on context: 'When debugging, show verbose output' or 'If this is a test file, use mocking patterns.' This creates intelligent rules that adapt to different situations within your project.
conditional_memory.whyItMatters: Conditional rules let Claude adapt its behavior based on context, providing more nuanced and situation-appropriate assistance.

howTo.summary: Use When/If/Only when/Unless patterns to create conditional instructions

steps.instruction: Identify situations that require different approaches
steps.note: Testing vs production, different file types, debugging, specific workflows

steps.instruction: Write conditional rules using clear trigger phrases

code.content:
## Conditional Guidelines

### When working with tests:
- Use Jest mock functions for external dependencies
- Follow AAA pattern (Arrange, Act, Assert)
- Name tests: 'should [expected behavior] when [condition]'

### If modifying API endpoints:
- Update the OpenAPI spec in /docs/openapi.yaml
- Add migration if database schema changes
- Update related integration tests

### Only when in production mode:
- Enable error tracking with Sentry
- Use minified bundles
- Enable CDN caching headers

steps.instruction: Use negative conditions when appropriate

code.content:
### Unless explicitly requested:
- Don't add comments explaining obvious code
- Don't create backup files
- Don't modify unrelated files

examples.title: Context-Aware Rules

code.content:
## Situational Guidelines

### When creating new components:
- Generate a test file alongside the component
- Add Storybook story if it's a UI component
- Export from the nearest index.ts barrel file

### If the file is in /src/legacy:
- Match existing code style (even if outdated)
- Don't refactor surrounding code
- Add TODO comments for future improvements

### When debugging issues:
- Add console.logs with [DEBUG] prefix
- Clean up debug statements before committing
- Check error boundaries are in place

examples.explanation: Conditional rules adapt Claude's behavior to match the current context.

tips: Keep conditions specific and unambiguous
Test that Claude correctly identifies when conditions apply

rule_maker.longDescription: Discover the .claude/rules/ directory for organizing modular rule files. Rule Maker introduces you to creating separate .md files in the rules directory, which Claude automatically loads alongside your CLAUDE.md. This is the first step toward a truly modular memory system where different rules can be maintained independently.
rule_maker.whyItMatters: The rules directory enables team members to contribute rules independently and keeps different concerns in separate, focused files.

howTo.summary: Create your first rule file in .claude/rules/

steps.instruction: Create your first rule file

code.content: touch .claude/rules/testing.md

steps.instruction: Add focused content to the rule file

code.content:
# Testing Rules

## Unit Tests
- Place tests next to source files: `foo.ts` -> `foo.test.ts`
- Use descriptive test names: 'should return null when input is empty'
- One assertion per test when possible

## Mocking
- Mock external dependencies, not internal modules
- Use jest.mock() at module level
- Reset mocks in beforeEach

## Coverage
- Minimum 80% coverage for new code
- Don't test implementation details

code.content:
# Git Workflow Rules

## Branches
- Feature branches: `feature/description`
- Bug fixes: `fix/description`
- Always branch from `main`

## Commits
- Use conventional commits: `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`
- Keep commits atomic and focused
- Write meaningful commit messages

## Pull Requests
- Require at least one review
- Squash merge to main
- Delete branch after merge

examples.title: Archaeological Record

code.content:
## Discovered Patterns

### Performance (Session 2024-01-18)
Discovered that our GraphQL queries were n+1 due to DataLoader not being initialized per-request. Solution: Create new DataLoader instance in context factory.

### Testing (Session 2024-01-12)
Found that our test database wasn't isolating transactions properly. Solution: Wrap each test in a transaction and rollback after.

### Deployment (Session 2024-01-08)
Cloud Run cold starts were 8s due to Prisma connection pooling. Solution: Use PgBouncer with transaction mode.

code.content:
## Our Patterns

### Service Layer Pattern
Business logic lives in service classes, not controllers.

### DTO Pattern
Data transfer objects validate and transform API data.

### Event Pattern
Use domain events for cross-module communication.

### Guard Pattern
Validate preconditions at function entry with early returns.

### Wrapper Pattern
Wrap third-party libraries for easier testing and migration.
